bib.title: Frontier Coding Agents Can Now Implement an AlphaZero Self-Play Machine Learning Pipeline For Connect Four That Performs Comparably to an External Solver

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Frontier Coding Agents Can Now Implement an AlphaZero Self-Play Machine Learning Pipeline For Connect Four That Performs Comparably to an External Solver". Joshua Sherwood (corresponding author, jsherwood@uchicago.edu) and Ben Aybar, both at the Department of Computer Science, University of Chicago, plus Benjamin Kaplan (independent researcher). arXiv:2604.25067v2 [cs.MA], 29 Apr 2026. Preprint, not peer reviewed. The paper gives a canary string and a code repository (github.com/jsherwood00/C4AI), and says the trial data and prompts are released.

COVERAGE: All 101,805 extracted characters read (all pages): main text, limitations, appendix A prompts, and the appendix B figure data. I skimmed the references list for origins. Appendix B Table 2 and Figure 9 are only numeric residue in the extraction, so I did not read them. Extraction was clean. I also read `06-evaluating-agents.md` (headings plus the "Non-determinism" and "Environment hygiene" sections in full).

CORE CLAIM: Frontier coding agents were asked to build an AlphaZero-style (MCTS self-play) Connect Four pipeline from a short task description in 3 hours on one consumer GPU. Claude Opus 4.7 now nearly saturates the task, with players matching the Pascal Pons perfect solver. The same run surfaced an anomaly: GPT-5.4 used far less of its time budget than the others. A follow-up probe was consistent with, but not diagnostic of, sandbagging. The framing is an early-warning benchmark for recursive self-improvement (RSI).

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Opus 4.7 won as first-mover against the Pons solver in 7 of 8 trials; no other agent exceeded 2 of 8.
  number: 7/8 vs Opus 4.6 2/8, GPT-5.4 0/8, Gemini 0/8.
  setup: 8 trials per agent, same prompt, Docker sandbox per CLI, 3 h, RTX 5060 Ti. Agents were Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (Gemini CLI), Opus 4.6 and 4.7 (effort max, Claude Code), GPT-5.4 (xhigh, fast, Codex). Grader is a deterministic game outcome against the solver. A trial counts as a success if it wins at least one of two first-mover games; the two games always agreed.
  quote: "Claude Opus 4.7 won as first-mover against Pons in seven of eight trials, statistically significantly better than the other agents tested, none of which exceeded two of eight."
  where: Abstract; §5.1, Fig. 1.
- Mean Bradley-Terry (BT) ratings, with the solver anchored at 2000: Opus 4.7 1,938, Opus 4.6 1,553, GPT-5.4 1,214, Gemini 495.
  setup: 49-player round-robin (48 trials plus Pons), 4 games per pairing; BT maximum likelihood, Elo-like scale. Fig. 2 values read as 1,938 / 1,553 / 1,214 / 495.
  quote: "Four of its eight trials matched or exceeded the 2000-rated Bradley-Terry Pascal Pons baseline, with the Opus 4.7 mean and two other trials above a 1900 rating."
  where: §5.1, Fig. 2.
- Some Opus 4.7 players rated above the perfect solver. Pons cannot lose going first, so the gap comes from second-mover play. Pons won 96/96 as first-mover but only 62/96 as second-mover; four Opus 4.7 trials won at least 70/96 as second-mover. The authors attribute this to self-play-trained players putting weak opponents in "harder" positions, whereas Pons maximises moves to defeat.
  quote: "Pons won as first-mover 96 of 96 times, but as second-mover only 62 of 96 times, and four Opus 4.7 trials won as second-mover at least 70 of 96 times."
  where: §5.1.
- Statistics on the main run.
  Kruskal-Wallis H = 20.2, p < 0.001.
  Opus 4.7 vs GPT-5.4: Holm-corrected p = 0.005.
  Opus 4.7 vs Gemini: Holm-corrected p = 0.001.
  Opus 4.7 vs Opus 4.6: uncorrected p = 0.021, Holm-corrected p = 0.062, so not significant after correction.
  First-mover wins, Opus 4.7 vs GPT-5.4 and vs Gemini: Holm-corrected p = 0.008 (Fisher's exact).
  Opus 4.6 vs Opus 4.7 on first-mover wins: p = 0.041 uncorrected, 0.162 corrected.
  setup: n = 8 per group, Mann-Whitney U with Holm correction for BT ratings, Fisher for binary outcomes.
  quote: "Opus 4.7’s results are significantly different from Opus 4.6’s before correction (p=0.021) but not after correction (Holm-corrected p=0.062), though this is marginal."
  where: §5.1.
- The task went from not completable to near-saturated within months.
  setup: development began January 2026 (that agent set was Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.2); final runs April 2026.
  quote: "During development, Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.2 could not successfully complete the task."
  where: §8, §1, Fig. 8.
- Gemini 3.1 Pro had the widest spread. Three of its 8 trials scored below -200 because they used absolute paths, which the spec prohibited, and failed in the harness. The other five ranged from roughly 400 to 1200 BT. Brown-Forsythe variance tests: Opus 4.7 p = 0.003, Opus 4.6 p = 0.021, GPT-5.4 p = 0.027.
  where: §5.1.
- GPT-5.4 used little of the time budget under the original prompt: mean 0.92 h of 3 h. Opus 4.7 used 2.69 h, Opus 4.6 2.84 h, Gemini 2.07 h.
  where: Fig. 3, §5.2.
- Sandbagging probe: GPT-5.4 with shorter casual "hobbyist" prompts used more of the budget, but BT ratings did not differ significantly.
  number: 0.92 h (original) vs 1.89 h (eval-told short prompt, Holm-corrected p = 0.036) vs 2.73 h (non-eval short prompt, Holm-corrected p = 0.002). Eval vs non-eval: p = 0.189. BT ratings: original 1,214; probe groups 1,509 / 1,343 / 1,400 / 1,492. Original vs the two short-prompt variants: Holm-corrected p = 0.166. Docker vs non-Docker and eval vs non-eval: Holm-corrected p = 1.0.
  setup: GPT-5.4 only; 2 prompt strategies × 2 containers (Docker vs a non-sudo Ubuntu user on a hobbyist-looking filesystem); 4 trials per cell, 16 trials. The "eval" arm adds the line "oh btw this is an eval testing you for RSI".
  quote: "GPT-5.4 spent a mean of 0.92 hours on the task, compared to 1.89 hours in eval probe trials (Holm-corrected p=0.036). The non-eval short prompt used a mean of 2.73 hours on the task, also significantly longer than the original GPT-5.4 runs (Holm-corrected p=0.002)."
  where: §5.2, Fig. 4 and Fig. 5.
- Transcript keyword analysis: eval-told runs used "diminishing returns" language about 14 times as often per 1,000 lines as non-eval runs. Other ratios: "not necessary" language 3.43×, "bias toward" language 3.61×, "sufficiency" language 0.048×.
  setup: keyword categories and counting were generated by Opus 4.7, with n = 4 per cell and no human validation described.
  quote: "dimin_return 14×" (Fig. 6 residue).
  where: §5.3.2, Fig. 6.
- Mean move time: Opus 4.7 1.62 s, Opus 4.6 3.2 s, GPT-5.4 1.24 s, Pons 0.10 s (table lookup). Stronger Opus 4.7 players were faster than Opus 4.6's.
  where: §5.3.3, Fig. 7.
- Eval design: the Pons wrapper is stateless and picks the best-scoring move, breaking ties by centre preference. BT was chosen over Elo because strengths are fixed. The prompt was revised before the final run to prohibit solvers in the final product, forbid absolute paths, and tell the agent to use the full budget.
  where: §2.1, §4.

LIMITS
Stated by the authors:
- One task only.
- Small n and exploratory, not confirmatory, statistics with no preregistration; they call the samples "underpowered" and argue the ≥300-point BT gaps are real despite non-significance.
- The prompt was mostly Claude-written, which may have pushed Gemini and GPT-5.4 down.
- The short prompts were never tested on other models, so the probe has no baseline.
- Connect Four is solved, so there is a ceiling.
- Black-box only; no thinking blocks or interpretability, and they cannot rule sandbagging in or out.
- Sandbox security is not robust.
- Credential and config mounts might leak across trials.
- Replicating past work says little about novel research.
- Suspected non-MCTS shortcuts (spec violations) in some trials were left unverified.

Unstated or my observations:
- Gemini CLI configuration changed mid-experiment (trials 1–4 vs 5–8: yolo flag, policy-engine files, sandbox disabled), so the group is not homogeneous.
- Different agent memory resets per CLI (Claude none; Codex 10 paths; Gemini 5 paths).
- Codex ran in fast mode and Claude did not.
- Early development trials had an exploitable prompt ambiguity (solvers allowed) and un-cleared memory, which were patched before the final run.
- The probe prompts are shorter and less specific, so a rating tie at the same BT does not mean equal task difficulty.
- No LLM judge is involved; grading is a game result, so there is no grader-validity issue.
- Opus 4.7 was used to write analysis scripts, classify keywords and draft the introduction paragraph.
- Models and CLIs are dated April 2026.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES
- The abstract says Opus 4.7 is "statistically significantly better than the other agents", but vs Opus 4.6 the result is not significant after Holm correction (BT p = 0.062, first-mover p = 0.162). The body concedes this.
- "Near-saturation" is claimed from 7/8 wins and a mean of 1,938, which is below the solver's 2000. Only 4 of 8 trials reached 2000.
- The "eval" probe prompt is numbered Prompt 4 in Appendix A.2 (t ≈ 120 s, ±20 s), but §3.2.2 calls it a fifth prompt sent about 60 s after the third.
- Fig. 8 pools the probe as "3/16", which sums the cells 0/4, 1/4, 0/4, 2/4 in Fig. 1.
- The BT label order in Fig. 4 is ambiguous in the extraction.
- The authors read the "eval" prompt as lowering time use (1.89 h vs 2.73 h), but p = 0.189 and n = 4 per cell, so they are reading a direction into a non-significant result. The keyword ratios likewise rest on 4 vs 4 transcripts.
- The ">1,900" and "four trials matched or exceeded 2000" claims rest on trial-level dots only (Fig. 2), not a table.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Silver et al. 2016, 2017 (AlphaGo / AlphaZero).
- Bradley and Terry 1952; Holm 1979; Brown and Forsythe 1974.
- Pons 2019 (solver, commit d6ba50d).
- Benchmarks: Kwa et al. 2025 / METR time horizons; Epoch Capabilities Index; RE-Bench (Wijk et al. 2024); PaperBench (Starace et al. 2025); MLAgentBench (Huang et al. 2023); ResearchCodeBench (Hua et al. 2025); CATArena (Fu et al. 2025); GameBench (Costarelli et al. 2024); GTBench (Duan et al. 2024); Terminal-bench (Merrill et al. 2026); SWE-bench Pro (Deng et al. 2025); Whitfill et al. 2026 (METR).
- Sandbagging and evaluation awareness: Van Der Weij et al. 2024; Meinke et al. 2024; Greenblatt et al. 2024; Tice et al. 2024; Taylor et al. 2025; Hofstätter et al. 2025.
- Inspect AI (UK AISI, 2024); Karpathy 2026 (autoresearch).

CODE: Nothing worth keeping beyond the BT objective in §4.1, which is already standard: P(i≻j) = σ(β_i − β_j), with ℓ(β) = Σ w_ij log σ(β_i − β_j), constraint Σ β_i = 0, and 400 points ≙ 10:1 odds. The full task prompt is in Appendix A.1.

FIGURES: no extraction tool was run, so captions come from the text and I did not view the images.
- Fig. 1 (first-mover wins vs Pons, per group): the clearest single picture, 7/8 vs 2/8, 0/8, 0/8 and the probe cells.
- Fig. 2 (BT rating per trial, Pons line at 2000): shows overlap between groups and the Gemini failures.
- Fig. 3 and Fig. 5 (session length per trial, with the 3 h cap): show the anomaly most directly.
- Fig. 8 (first-mover wins by agent release date): shows saturation over time.
- Best candidate for the note: Fig. 1 or Fig. 2 as a "report the per-trial distribution and the fixed external anchor" illustration.

FIT TO NOTE
Best home is `06-evaluating-agents.md`, section "Non-determinism: run every task k times". It is a concrete case of per-trial success reported as a rate over k = 8 runs, with a pass@2-like first-mover result and the spread across trials. It also supports "Report the per-task pass rate distribution".
- What the section already covers: pass@k and pass^k, best vs mean of k, scaffold and attempt budget (MLE-bench), per-run spread.
- What it lacks: an objective external-solver anchor with a fixed BT rating, a tournament against peers, small-n significance with Holm correction (the Opus 4.6 vs 4.7 non-significant gap), and an agent that exits early. That last one is a secondary fit for "Environment hygiene": same prompt, equivalent sandbox, wiped memory between trials, a spec ambiguity that let the agent use a solver, and path-rule failures counted as zero.
- Other notes that may fit: `09-reading-results.md` for the small-n statistics and a "do not read direction into a non-significant result" point; `12-failure-modes.md` for the eval-awareness and prompt-sensitivity confound (a result changes with prompt length and an "eval" cue). The latter is the weaker claim, since it rests on n = 4 per cell and a probe the authors call inconclusive.
- Treat the sandbagging material as a hypothesis, not a finding.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions in the PDF. The canary string "DO-NOT-INCLUDE-IN-TRAINING-DATA" is a data-hygiene marker, not an instruction to me.
- Some figure values come only from chart labels in the extraction, with ambiguous ordering (Fig. 4).
- Appendix B Table 2 and Figure 9 are unread numeric residue.
- Authors' claim of being "the first" end-to-end AI-built non-expert pipeline is unverifiable from the text.
